Reverted from main on the owner's instruction so the other three merged branches could ship green. The processing record failed e2e in WebKit at a roughly 50 percent rate: --repeat-each=6 gave 3 failed and 3 passed, and a passing run recorded requestsDuringJob 1 correctly, so this was never a deterministic bug and my first report calling it reproducible was wrong. The cause is a limit in what the measurement can promise rather than a coding slip. A Resource Timing entry is only created when a load completes, but the record's declared window is requests started during the job. The single page request in this job is the PDF worker script and the job lasts about 29ms, so when that load has not finished at snapshot time no entry exists and the request is invisible; the record then reports requestsDuringJob 0 for a job that did make a request. The complete flag does not catch it because it is derived only from resource-timing buffer overflow, never from requests still in flight, so the record can state measured true, complete true and a count of zero while being wrong. On a product whose pitch is that nothing leaves the device, a confident zero is the most load-bearing claim it could get wrong, which is why this was not shipped and not papered over by relaxing the assertion. The test is correct to demand the record match observed reality; that agreement is the feature. Nothing was discarded: the work remains on branch claude/attestation and is recoverable, and the original ledger entry for building it is left in place because this file is append-only. Fixing it means changing the measurement contract, either collecting entries that arrive after the window through a PerformanceObserver and deferring the snapshot, or stating plainly that loads in flight at measurement time are not counted and setting complete false. Also noted for whoever picks it up: lib/attestation/network.ts carried two raw NUL bytes used as composite map-key separators, written as literal bytes instead of a unicode escape, which is why git recorded it as binary and plain grep refused to match it.

Business rule 23 permits a measured egress claim only for a build that passed the current egress proof protocol, but that protocol existed only as a reference: ai/KNOWN_ISSUES.md recorded it as not empirically complete and implementation/ARCHITECTURE.md said that because of it the UI says proof is pending. The UI did not say pending. The deployed bundle carried zero cloud uploads, zero data leaks, zero third-party cloud uploads and 100 percent on your device. The owner asked for this to be settled before any launch, which is the right sequence, because the audiences that would fund this product are precisely the audiences that open devtools and check. Rather than soften everything, the claim was measured. e2e/egress-proof.spec.ts is now the protocol and runs on the production build in both engines Playwright drives. It checks three things in increasing order of strength: that the served policy forbids connections, that five deliberate exfiltration attempts from the page's own context are refused, and that a real PNG through a real tool produces no off-origin response, zero off-origin bytes, no request carrying a body, no filename in any request URL and no fetch, xhr, beacon or websocket initiator at all. Six of six pass. The detector was then proved non-vacuous by pointing it at a page that genuinely loads a cross-origin resource, where it fails and catches one response and six hundred and eighteen bytes; a proof that cannot fail establishes nothing. Two traps surfaced that would each silently invert a result and are now documented. A navigator.sendBeacon blocked by CSP still returns true, because the specification returns true once the beacon is queued and the policy refuses it afterwards, so any check asserting on that return value records a leak as a pass. And Chromium raises a request event for a request it is about to block, reporting failure reason csp with zero bytes transferred, where WebKit raises nothing at all, so a check asserting that nothing was attempted fails Chromium on a page behaving perfectly. The protocol therefore asserts that no off-origin request received a response and that zero bytes were transferred, which is both correct and stronger. Because the egress claim is now earned it was kept and strengthened to name the mechanism a sceptic can verify in devtools in ten seconds, connect-src none, which is a better sentence than the adjective it replaced. Two claims were removed because no egress proof can ever earn them: zero data leaks and prevented accidental data leaks are security guarantees, assertions about every vulnerability that does not exist, whereas egress evidence reports only where bytes went; and saved you paid software subscriptions is a claim about the reader's money, which is an invented number by another name under board section 1.7. Both are guarded in lib/seo/live-tools.test.ts and the guard was verified by reintroducing zero data leaks and watching the suite go red. One open item for the owner: Cloudflare injects its analytics beacon into the HTML at the edge with a data-cf-beacon token, and the site's own CSP blocks it so nothing is collected today, transfer size zero and none of its globals present, but the claim survives only because the policy catches it and it should be turned off at source in the zone's Browser Insights setting.

Portals say MB without saying whether they mean MB or MiB, so decimalMbToKib reads the stated figure as decimal and rounds down to whole KiB, keeping a conforming file under the ceiling on either reading. presetsOverdue() backs the gate and the gate was proven rather than assumed: dating a row 2026-01-01 turns the suite red on exactly that test and only that test. Decision 16's expiry rule was written to catch limits that drift; its first run caught limits that were never right, so requiring a source did more work here than requiring a date.
